strengths: Novel and well-motivated core idea: adaptive canonicalization depending on network predictive confidence elegantly addresses known discontinuity issues in standard canonicalization

Strong theoretical contributions: Theorems 6-13 rigorously establish continuity, symmetry preservation, and universal approximation properties; Theorem 9 explicitly proves adaptive canonicalization is continuous while standard canonicalization is not
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple domains (graphs, molecules, point clouds) with consistent improvements over equivariant architectures and standard canonicalization
Good ablation studies (sampling vs. optimization, graph vs. node-level, out-of-distribution generalization) and additional analysis in appendix
Clear presentation with intuitive motivation (horse classifier example) and rigorous mathematical framework at appropriate generality
weaknesses: Significant theory-practice gap: Theorem 9 assumes continuous prior maximization but practical implementations use sampling-based or sample-and-refine optimization that may not satisfy this exactly; gap between infinite-width UAT and finite practical networks not addressed

Computational complexity not analyzed: Acknowledged requirement of D optimization problems at test time (one per class) has no runtime comparisons with baselines; Table 5 shows sampling methods need 5-10× candidates for competitive accuracy, raising scalability concerns

Restricted to classification tasks: Acknowledged limitation not addressed; unclear how framework extends to regression, structured prediction, or generation tasks; one-vs-rest setup appears specific to classification

Weak practical guidance: No clear principles for selecting prior functions H; sensitivity analysis w.r.t. prior choice absent; practitioners lack guidance on when to use adaptive vs. standard canonicalization

Statistical rigor concerns: Several improvements modest and within error margins (e.g., PROTEINS 85.47±0.8 vs 83.41±1.4); grid signal task explicitly designed to showcase orientation sensitivity; hyperparameter tuning details sparse (Optuna search spaces may not be equivalent across methods)

Incomplete experimental comparisons: Limited comparison with recent learned canonicalization methods on all benchmarks; modern equivariant methods (e.g., for point clouds) not compared; OGB results compare against 'reported results from prior work' with potentially different experimental protocols
Definition 4's equicontinuity condition somewhat abstract; why this specific uniformity requirement? Intuition and motivation could be clearer
Missing ablation: Paper claims Ψ benefits from being symmetryless but this is not explicitly ablated; design choice not validated empirically
Unaddressed failure modes: No discussion of when adaptive canonicalization is not beneficial or what problem characteristics favor/disfavor the approach

strengths: Addresses genuine problem: the discontinuity of standard canonicalization is well-documented (Dym et al. 2024) and the paper provides a principled solution
Solid theoretical framework: rigorous definitions, correct proofs, and novel characterization of output space as symmetry-preserving functions (Theorem 12)
Clear motivation: the horse/image example effectively illustrates adaptive canonicalization vs. standard approaches
Mathematically sound: elegant treatment of quotient spaces and proper use of equicontinuity in universal approximation theorems
weaknesses: Substantial theory-practice gap: theoretical guarantees assume exact maximization over transformations, but practice uses approximate sample-and-refine heuristics without convergence analysis or approximation rates

Computational efficiency inadequately addressed: acknowledged need to solve D optimizations at runtime (critical for inference), but no wall-clock time analysis, FLOPs, or scalability comparisons provided

Modest and inconsistent empirical results: improvements typically 1-3% on standard benchmarks (e.g., AC-DGCNN 91.7% vs CN-DGCNN 90.0%; MUTAG 87.94% vs OAP 84.95%), often within noise margins, no statistical significance testing
Toy problem is circular: grid signal orientation task (99.38% accuracy) is essentially designed for the method's specific capability; doesn't demonstrate real-world utility

Disconnect between abstract framework and concrete applications: unclear why per-sample optimization of orthogonal transformations in A-NLSF is fundamentally superior to standard canonicalization; connection to abstract theory is obscured by dense technical presentation

Anisotropy claims unjustified: claiming A-NLSF/AC-networks are 'anisotropic' because non-equivariant Ψ can exploit different directions is already true for any standard canonicalization; core difference is just per-input optimization, which is a weaker novelty claim
Significant scope limitations: regression tasks not addressed despite claiming to be a 'general framework'; one-vs-rest classification formulation less natural than softmax
Missing critical ablations: prior function h_d choice/sensitivity, sample-and-refine hyperparameters (# samples, # GD steps), limited distribution shift evaluation
Joint optimization not analyzed: no discussion of convergence properties, initialization, or landscape of jointly optimizing ρ_f and network weights during training
Technical ambiguities: ties in argmax (Eq. 2) handling glossed over; equicontinuity verification in practice not discussed; Theorem 8 proof extends D=1 to D>1 without full justification

strengths: Novel framework addressing a real limitation of standard canonicalization (discontinuities affecting stability and generalization). The core idea of network-dependent canonicalization via prior maximization is well-motivated and intuitive.

Strong theoretical development with rigorous proofs. Proves continuity of end-to-end models (Theorem 9), establishes universal approximation properties (Theorems 6, 13), and elegantly characterizes the connection to symmetry-preserving functions (Theorem 12).

Comprehensive experimental validation across diverse domains (TUDataset, OGB molecular benchmarks, ModelNet40) with consistent improvements over multiple baselines (equivariant networks, standard canonicalization, frame averaging).
Two well-developed concrete applications (A-NLSF for spectral GNNs, point cloud networks) showing technical depth and non-trivial instantiation of the framework.
Excellent presentation of core intuition (horse orientation example). Toy problem clearly demonstrates the method's advantage (99.38% vs. ~50% for baselines).
Extensive reproducibility materials including detailed implementation specifications, hyperparameter searches, and ablation studies (sampling vs. optimization-based approaches).
Rigorous mathematical framework that elegantly unifies diverse symmetries (permutations, rotations, eigenbasis selection) through the equicontinuity property.
weaknesses: Computational efficiency concerns unaddressed: Method requires D optimization problems at runtime for D classes. No wall-clock time comparisons provided. For large D (e.g., 128 classes in ogbg-molpcba) or at inference time, overhead could be substantial. Sample-and-refine approach is a workaround, not a principled solution.

Limited scope: Framework restricted to classification tasks only. Regression mentioned as future work. This significantly limits applicability in scientific/continuous prediction domains. One-vs-rest design seems specific to classification.

Theoretical contributions are confirmatory rather than deep: Theorems mostly verify expected properties (continuity, UAT) rather than providing surprising insights. No generalization bounds, sample complexity analysis, or theoretical explanation for when/why adaptive canonicalization outperforms equivariant architectures (which also provide continuity).

Modest empirical improvements on some benchmarks: OGB improvements ~0.7-1.2% over strong baselines (GPS, SAN); PROTEINS: 85.47% vs 83.41% (OAP+GIN). Toy problem is artificial and unrepresentative of real data structure. Some benchmarks show <1% gap to best baseline.

Incomplete analysis of design choices: One-vs-rest setup with D independent priors seems ad-hoc. Sensitivity to prior function h_d not analyzed. Performance degradation with large D not empirically shown. Fundamental difference from learned canonicalization (Kaba et al. 2023) unclear.

Missing critical experimental analysis: (1) No scaling analysis vs. number of classes D; (2) No computational cost (FLOPs/time) comparisons; (3) Limited interpretability—what patterns do learned orientations capture; (4) Ablations on prior choice, band selection in A-NLSF incomplete.

Presentation issues: Dense mathematical exposition (especially Definitions 10-11 with 'galaxies' formalism) makes paper hard to follow. 'Anisotropic' terminology overloaded. Connection between general framework and applications could be more explicit. Limited discussion of when/why method succeeds or fails.

Experimental design: (1) ModelNet40 uses on-the-fly rotation augmentation during training (somewhat artificial); (2) Out-of-distribution evaluation (z/SO(3)) relegated to appendix; (3) Sample-and-refine optimization not differentiated through backpropagation—impact unclear; (4) Toy problem oversimplified.

Limited discussion of practical impact of discontinuity claim: While standard canonicalization is theoretically discontinuous, the practical effect on real benchmarks is unclear. Do observed improvements actually correlate with continuity? Not empirically validated.

strengths: Novel theoretical contribution: Making canonicalization depend on the network (not just input) solves the recognized continuity problem in standard canonicalization approaches
Rigorous mathematical framework with proper treatment of equicontinuity, universal approximation theorems, and symmetry-preservation guarantees (Theorems 6, 9, 12-13)

Comprehensive experimental validation across multiple domains (graphs, point clouds) with consistent improvements over equivariant architectures, data augmentation, and standard canonicalization baselines
Well-motivated with compelling intuition from cognitive psychology (mental rotation); clear presentation of complex theoretical material
General framework not limited to group actions; handles arbitrary transformation families and provides detailed implementation guidance
weaknesses: Significant gap between theory and practice: Theoretical guarantees assume true maximization, but practical implementation uses sampling-based approximation with local refinement (Alg. 1); empirical quality of approximation not thoroughly evaluated
Modest practical improvements relative to added complexity: 1-4% gains over strong baselines; computational cost of D runtime optimizations not fully justified by performance gains

Limited scope of applications: A-NLSF addresses eigenbasis ambiguity handled by other recent methods; point cloud networks combine existing architectures; segmentation requires modifications that lose continuity guarantees
Insufficient comparison with related work: Weighted frame averaging (Dym et al. 2024) also achieves continuity; detailed comparison relegated to appendix; no direct empirical comparison
Method primarily limited to classification tasks; extension to regression unexplored, limiting applicability
Multiple hyperparameters introduced without sufficient guidance on selection (K samples, refinement steps, band partitioning); sensitivity analysis in G.5 is limited
Statistical significance testing largely absent from experimental results; no confidence intervals or formal hypothesis tests for claimed improvements
